source.title_on_document: Can ChatGPT enhance business student creativity? Evidence from a randomised controlled trial

supplement.where: The article refers to no supplementary material or online appendix.

paper_design_summary: First-year undergraduate business students in 26 classes in three disciplines (Entrepreneurship, Marketing, Management) were randomly assigned within discipline to use ChatGPT-3.5 or to work without generative AI (usual resources, including internet search) on a 15-minute Alternative Uses-type task: uses for a paperclip (Entrepreneurship and Marketing) or ideas to return employees to the workplace (Management). Three raters scored each submission for fluency (idea count), flexibility, originality, and elaboration; flexibility was dropped from the analysis, and the other three were analyzed by MANOVA, one for Entrepreneurship plus Marketing and one for Management.

studies.label: Entrepreneurship and Marketing students, paperclip alternative-uses task (first MANOVA)

assignment.what_was_assigned: ChatGPT-3.5 access during the ideation task (experiment) versus instructed not to use any generative AI (control), within discipline
assignment.quote: Students were randomly assigned to either the control group or the experiment (ChatGPT-3.5) group within each discipline and before their respective class.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 7 (journal p. 1437), Description of participants and sampling

arms.name: ChatGPT-3.5, Entrepreneurship
arms.description: Given access to ChatGPT-3.5 and instructed to interact with it to generate ideas; watched a 2-minute prompting video; paperclip uses task

arms.name: Control, Entrepreneurship
arms.description: Generated ideas independently using usual resources (discipline materials, personal knowledge, internet searches); told not to use generative AI; paperclip uses task

participants.exclusions: The paper gives n = 160 (Entrepreneurship, 3 elective classes) and n = 496 (Marketing, 12 core classes) as the recruited participants (656 together), before removal of duplicate students attending two subjects, non-consenting students, incomplete submissions, outliers, and two multivariate outliers. It never states how many were randomized to each arm or analyzed. The printed degrees of freedom (Pillai F(3, 196); univariate F(1, 198)) suggest roughly 200 students analyzed in this MANOVA, but the paper does not state the count.

outcomes.name: Fluency (count of ideas per respondent)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of the total number of ideas each respondent generated, recorded by three raters; inter-rater Pearson rs = .83-.95. How the three raters' counts were combined is not stated.

contrasts.reported: Univariate main effect of intervention: F(1,198) = 0.14, p = .70. Intervention x discipline interaction: F(1, 198) = 8.89, p = .003, partial eta2 = .04.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 9 (journal p. 1439) and PDF p. 10 (journal p. 1440), Results, Entrepreneurship and marketing students

contrasts.reported: Control 3.22 (0.23) vs Intervention 3.11 (0.23); Significance .752. Values in parentheses are not labeled (SD or SE); no arm ns.
Control 2.52 (0.16) vs Intervention 3.65 (0.20); Significance <.001. Values in parentheses are not labeled; no arm ns.

outcomes.name: Originality (rubric rating, 5-point scale)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three raters with practical and theoretical experience of the three domains rated uniqueness of ideas compared with what each rater saw in the overall sample, on a 5-point rubric scale (Exceptional to Insufficient); inter-rater Pearson rs = .32-.49. Aggregation across raters not stated.

contrasts.reported: The intervention group scored significantly higher in originality than the control group (F(1,198) = 25.62, p < .001). Interaction with discipline: F(1, 198) = 3.80, p = .053, partial eta2 = .019.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 9 (journal p. 1439) and PDF p. 10 (journal p. 1440), Results

outcomes.name: Elaboration (rubric rating, 5-point scale)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Degree of detail, specificity, and richness of ideas, rated by the three raters on the 5-point rubric; inter-rater Pearson rs = .60-.66.

contrasts.reported: Univariate main effect of intervention: F(1, 198) = 0.001, p = .974. Interaction with discipline: F(1, 198) = 17.23, p < .001, partial eta2 = .08.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 9 (journal p. 1439) and PDF p. 10 (journal p. 1440), Results

outcomes.name: Flexibility (variety of categories of ideas), measured but dropped
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Variety of different categories of ideas, rated by the three raters with the rubric; inter-rater rs > .75-.88. Dropped from the analysis because of a very strong correlation with fluency; no results reported.

contrasts.reported: Not reported; the paper states fluency and flexibility produce essentially identical outcomes.

eligibility.reason: Students were randomly assigned within discipline to ChatGPT-3.5 or no generative AI (p. 7); outputs were rated by three raters for fluency, originality, and elaboration (p. 8). The paper never states analyzed counts: it gives 656 recruited for S1 and 534 for S2, and the printed degrees of freedom imply roughly 200 and 120 analyzed, both well above 50. Control students could use internet search as part of their usual resources, so the contrast is coded ai_vs_bau.

one_line_finding: ChatGPT-3.5 raised Marketing students' fluency (3.65 vs 2.52), originality (1.14 vs 0.79), and elaboration (1.50 vs 0.80), raised Management students' fluency (2.29 vs 1.78) and elaboration (1.99 vs 1.06) but not originality (p = .064), and had no detectable effect for Entrepreneurship students (PDF p. 10, Tables 1 and 2).
open_questions: Analyzed counts per arm and per study are not stated anywhere; only recruitment counts (160, 496, 534; 1190 total) and MANOVA degrees of freedom are printed. Whether the 1190 recruited students were all randomized (before consent and data cleaning) is unclear.
Parenthetical values in Tables 1 and 2 are not labeled as SD or SE; no arm ns are printed.

The pooled Entrepreneurship+Marketing univariate tests (fluency F = 0.14, p = .70; originality F = 25.62, p < .001) seem hard to reconcile with Table 1, where Marketing fluency differs at p < .001 and Entrepreneurship originality does not differ.
Management originality is reported as F(1,198) although the other Management tests use 120 error df.
Control condition allowed internet search as part of usual resources; a reviewer may prefer ai_vs_active.
How the three raters' scores were combined into one score per student is not stated.
notes: Multivariate results: S1 Pillai's trace = 0.06, F(3, 196) = 4.63, p = .004, partial eta2 = .06 for intervention; discipline Pillai 0.19, F(3,196) = 15.31; intervention x discipline Pillai .09, F(3,196) = 6.75, p < .001 (PDF p. 9). S2 Wilks Lambda = .07, F(3, 118) = 19.92, p < .001, partial eta2 = .33 (PDF p. 10). Two multivariate outliers removed (chi2(4) = 18.46). Box's M significant for the first MANOVA, so Pillai's trace reported. 26 classes, five researchers administered the task. No diversity-across-people outcome is reported.
